## John 13 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

John 13 begins the second major section of John's Gospel (the "Return to the Father," 13:1–20:29). Chapters 13–17 form Jesus' Farewell Discourse, delivered in the Upper Room on the night before His crucifixion. John omits the institution of the Lord's Supper (covered by the Synoptics) but uniquely records the foot-washing and extended dialogue. Warren Wiersbe outlines three lessons: Humility (vv. 1–5), Holiness (vv. 6–17), and Hypocrisy (vv. 18–38). The Greek words for "love" (*agapē*/*agapaō*) occur only 8 times in chapters 1–12 but 31 times in chapters 13–17.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-13-commentary

---

### v. 1 — The Hour and the Love

**Traditional Reading:** "Before the feast of the Passover" gives a time reference. Scholars debate whether this meal was on the actual Passover or the day before. Jesus "knew that His hour had come" — throughout John's Gospel He had been protected because His hour "had not yet come" (2:4, 7:30, 8:20); now it has arrived. His death is described gently as a "departure" to the Father. The phrase "He loved them to the end" (Greek *eis telos*) means "to the uttermost," "to the fullest extent" — not merely temporal endurance but the complete outpouring of love. The cross casts its shadow over every word.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-13/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-13-commentary

**Gill:** The "hour" was a fixed time, just as there was a "fulness of time" for His coming. "His own" means the elect, those given Him by the Father and purchased by His blood. "To the end" (*eis telos*) can mean "continually" or "forever."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/13.htm

**Catholic reading:** The timing note ("before the feast") supports John's chronology that this was the day before the official Passover, which is why Eastern churches use leavened bread for the Eucharist (the meal being an ordinary meal), while Western churches use unleavened bread (treating it as a genuine Passover).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-13/

---

### v. 2 — Judas's Heart and Satan's Role

**Traditional Reading:** "Supper being ended" is probably better translated "supper was now in progress" (a one-letter difference in Greek manuscripts: *genomenou* vs. *ginomenou*). The devil had already put the impulse to betray Jesus into Judas's heart — some read it as the devil having "made up his mind" about using Judas.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-13/

**Gill** argues this supper was at Bethany two days before Passover, not the Passover meal itself. He notes it was while the ointment was poured on Jesus' head and Judas was fretting at its cost that Satan took advantage of his anger.
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/13.htm

---

### v. 3 — Jesus' Knowledge of His Authority

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus knew three things: (1) the Father had given all things into His hands; (2) He had come from God; (3) He was returning to God. This knowledge of His divine authority and identity is precisely what enabled His humble service — not in spite of His greatness, but because of it. It was important that Jesus faced the cross as victor, not victim.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-13/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-13-commentary

**Gill:** Christ's sense of His own greatness as Mediator — having all persons, blessings, and authority in His hands — illustrates the wonder of His condescension.
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/13.htm

---

### vv. 4–5 — Jesus Washes the Disciples' Feet

**Traditional Reading:** John's account reads like an eyewitness report — short, vivid, staccato sentences. Jesus rose from supper, laid aside His outer garments, wrapped a towel around His waist, poured water, and began washing feet. This was the job of the lowest household servant. It was unthinkable in Jewish tradition for a teacher to wash disciples' feet. Luke 22:24 notes the disciples had been arguing about who was greatest; no one had volunteered to wash feet. Jesus' actions are a "living parable" prefiguring the cross: He rose from His throne, laid aside His glory, took the form of a servant, and poured out His blood to cleanse.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-13/

**Gill:** The towel/linen cloth was a servile garment; servants stood at their masters' feet girded with linen. The basin used for foot-washing was prescribed by Jewish tradition to hold between two logs and nine kabs of water. It was a servile work ordinarily done by inferiors for superiors — wife for husband, son for father, servant for master.
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/13.htm

---

### vv. 6–8 — Peter's Objection

**Traditional Reading:** Peter's "Lord, are You going to wash my feet?" expresses shock that the Master would stoop to this. Jesus replies that Peter will understand "later" — after the cross and resurrection. Peter's "Never shall You wash my feet!" is described as "proud humility" (Trapp) or "immoderate modesty." Jesus' response — "Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me" — shows that fellowship with Christ depends not on achieving something but on receiving His cleansing work. The literal foot-washing was not the essential point (Judas had his feet washed but had "no part" with Jesus); the acceptance of Christ's lowly service is what matters.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-13/

**Gill:** Jesus uses "wash" not literally but mystically — meaning washing by His blood and Spirit. "No part with Me" means no fellowship or communion, not loss of being "in" Christ.
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/13.htm

---

### vv. 9–11 — Peter's Overcorrection and "Bathed vs. Washed"

**Traditional Reading:** Peter swings from refusal to demanding a full bath. Jesus teaches that one who has been bathed (Greek *louō*) needs only to wash his feet (Greek *niptō*). This pictures the distinction between the once-for-all cleansing of salvation (the "bath") and the ongoing daily cleansing from sin ("foot-washing"). Spurgeon compared it to the Old Testament priest: consecrated by a full washing, then washing hands and feet at the laver before each service.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-13/

**Gill:** "He that is washed" means one regenerated by the Spirit or washed in Christ's blood. Such a person is "clean every whit" — forensically justified, all sins pardoned. Yet the "feet" of life and conversation continually gather dirt and need daily washing.
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/13.htm

**Catholic reading (Orchard):** Many Gk and Vg manuscripts lack "but" and "his feet," so the sense is simply: one who has bathed needs no further partial washing. Jesus passes to the moral sense: "You are clean, but not all."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/boc/john-13.html

---

### vv. 12–15 — The Example of Humble Service

**Traditional Reading:** After resuming His place, Jesus asks, "Do you know what I have done to you?" He affirms they rightly call Him Teacher and Lord, and draws the lesson: "If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet." Verse 15: "I have set you an example, so that you should do as I have done for you."

**Denominational Difference — Foot-Washing as Ordinance:**

This is one of the most debated passages across Protestant traditions:

- **Most Protestants (Baptist, Reformed, Methodist, Lutheran, Anglican, Pentecostal):** The command is about the principle of humble service, not a literal ritual. Constable's Notes argue that Jesus called this an "example" (Greek *hypodeigma*, "pattern"), implying other examples of the same attitude; nowhere else does the NT treat foot-washing as an ordinance; 1 Timothy 5:10 lists it among good works of humble service, not as a sacrament. Dr. Constable adds: "If Jesus were giving an example in modern North American culture, He probably would have selected another humble act."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/john-13.html

- **Grace Brethren, certain Mennonite churches, Church of the Brethren, and some Baptist groups:** Practice literal foot-washing as a third ordinance alongside baptism and the Lord's Supper (often called "Love Feast"). They cite vv. 14–15, 17 and the "ought" (*opheilō* — "are bound") as evidence. The Church of the Brethren practices the "Single Mode" where each person washes and wipes another's feet in connection with the Agape meal and Communion.
  — https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/isb/w/washing-of-feet.html

- **Catholic:** The Church keeps foot-washing in the liturgy of Holy Thursday (Maundy Thursday) but has never regarded it as a sacrament or permanent sacramental. It is "a generic example" of humble service. Some Church Fathers (Ambrose, Bernard) saw the foot-washing as mystically signifying the purity required for receiving the Eucharist.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/boc/john-13.html

- **Lapide (Catholic commentator):** Argues the foot-washing was a "sacramental ablution" preparing the apostles for reception of the Eucharist, converting an ordinary custom into a sacred ceremony.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/clc/john-13.html

---

### vv. 16–17 — The Servant Not Greater Than His Master

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus reinforces with a double "Amen" ("Truly, truly") that no servant is greater than his master, nor messenger greater than the sender. This addresses the disciples' earlier dispute about greatness (Luke 22:24). "If you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them" — blessing comes from *doing*, not merely knowing.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-13/

**Gill:** The beatitude is conditional: knowledge must be accompanied by practice; it is "the practice of such an example that brings the happiness of true discipleship."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/13.htm

---

### vv. 18–19 — The Betrayer Foretold from Scripture

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus clarifies He is not speaking of all — He knows whom He has chosen. He quotes Psalm 41:9: "The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me." The betrayal fulfills Scripture. Verse 19 shows Jesus' foreknowledge serves an evidential purpose: "so that when it comes to pass, you will believe that I AM He" — the "I am" formula echoing the divine name.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-13/

---

### v. 20 — Receiving the Sent Ones

**Traditional Reading:** A chain of representation: receiving Jesus' messengers = receiving Jesus = receiving the Father. This connects the apostolic mission to divine authority.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-13/

---

### vv. 21–26 — The Betrayer Identified

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus becomes "troubled in spirit" — one of only a few instances where His inner emotional turmoil is recorded (cf. 11:33, 12:27). He testifies that one of the Twelve will betray Him. The disciples are perplexed. "The disciple whom Jesus loved" (John) reclines at Jesus' side. Peter motions to John to ask who it is. Jesus identifies the betrayer as the one to whom He gives the dipped morsel — and gives it to Judas. This was an act of honor at a meal, making it a final appeal of love and an opportunity for repentance.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-13/

**Catholic reading (Orchard):** The dipped morsel indicates the supper was not yet finished — implying the Eucharist had not yet been instituted at this point.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/boc/john-13.html

---

### vv. 27–30 — Satan Enters Judas; He Departs

**Traditional Reading:** When Judas takes the morsel, "Satan entered into him." Jesus tells him, "What you are about to do, do quickly." The disciples misunderstand, thinking Judas (the group's treasurer) was sent to buy supplies for the feast or give to the poor. Judas "went out into the night" — John notes this with symbolic weight: it was literally and spiritually night.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-13/

---

### vv. 31–32 — The Glorification Begins

**Traditional Reading:** Once Judas departs, Jesus declares, "Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in Him." The departure of Judas signals that the betrayal and crucifixion are now irreversible — and in that impending death lies Christ's glory. The cross is not shame but exaltation. A mutual glorification occurs: the Son glorifies the Father through His obedience; the Father glorifies the Son "at once."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-13/

**Ellicott:** The brightness of the vision overpowers all thought of the darkness of the path leading to it. The glory "lies so immediately before Him that it is at once realised."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/13.htm

---

### v. 33 — "Little Children, Where I Am Going You Cannot Come"

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus addresses them tenderly as "little children" (*teknia*) — the only time this term appears in the Gospels (though frequent in 1 John). He echoes what He told the Jews (7:33–34; 8:21): where He is going, they cannot come — yet with a different implication for the disciples, who will follow later (v. 36).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-13/

---

### vv. 34–35 — The New Commandment

**Traditional Reading:** "A new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another." The Greek word for "new" (*kainos*) implies freshness or a new quality, not merely something recently invented. The command to love one's neighbor was not new (Lev. 19:18); what is new is the standard: "as I have loved you" — a self-sacrificial love modeled on the cross. Verse 35: mutual love among disciples is the visible, public mark that identifies them as Jesus' followers — the world's apologetic.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-13/

---

### vv. 36–38 — Peter's Denial Predicted

**Traditional Reading:** Peter ignores the new commandment and focuses on Jesus' destination: "Lord, where are You going?" Jesus answers he cannot follow now but "will follow later" (a promise of eventual restoration and martyrdom, cf. 21:18–19). Peter boasts, "I will lay down my life for You." Jesus exposes this as emotionally driven devotion: "Will you lay down your life for Me? Truly, truly, I tell you, before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times." Peter's confidence would crumble; "a servant-girl's tongue was sharper than an executioner's sword."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-13/

---

### Key Denominational & Theological Distinctives Identified

| Issue | Positions |
|---|---|
| **Foot-washing as ordinance** | Most Protestants: principle of humble service. Grace Brethren/Mennonites/Church of the Brethren: third ordinance. Catholic: liturgical rite on Maundy Thursday, not a sacrament. |
| **Timing relative to Passover** | John places it "before the feast"; Synoptics seem to place it on Passover. This affects whether the Last Supper was a Passover meal (Western view, unleavened bread) or the night before (Eastern view, leavened bread). |
| **"Bathed vs. washed" (v. 10)** | Generally understood across traditions as the distinction between once-for-all salvation cleansing and ongoing daily cleansing from sin. Catholic commentators (e.g., Augustine, Ambrose) connect foot-washing mystically to Eucharistic purity. |
| **Judas at the Eucharist** | Debate among Catholic commentators whether Judas received the Eucharist or departed before its institution. Lapide argues the foot-washing and prediction of betrayal preceded the Eucharist; Orchard notes the morsel indicates the Eucharist had not yet been instituted. |
